course.name: Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II

question.text:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle x,\: y,\: 2z\rangle$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2x+3y$ for $0\leq x\leq 1$ and $0\leq y\leq 1.$ Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n.$

Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||\mathbf r_x \times \mathbf r_y|| = \sqrt{14}.$
question.explanation:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S. \]

Notice that our surface $z = 2x+3y$ can be written using the dot product as

\[ \langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle -2,\: -3, \: 1\rangle}_{\widetilde{\mathbf n}} = 0, \quad \textrm{or}\quad \langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle 2,\: 3, \: -1\rangle}_{-\widetilde{\mathbf n}}= 0. \]

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

\[ \widetilde{\mathbf n} = \langle -2,\, -3,\, 1\rangle. \]

Normalizing this vector, we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf n &= \dfrac{\widetilde{\mathbf n}}{\Vert \widetilde{\mathbf n} \Vert} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\langle -2,\, -3,\, 1\rangle}{\sqrt{(-2)^2+(-3)^2+1^2}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{14}}\langle -2,\, -3,\, 1\rangle. \end{align*}

Using the fact that $z=2x+3y$ on $S,$ we have

\begin{align} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} &= \left\langle x,\: y,\: 2z \right\rangle \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{14}}\langle -2,\, -3,\, 1\rangle\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{14}} \left\langle x,\: y,\: 4x+6y \right\rangle \cdot \langle -2,\, -3,\, 1\rangle\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{14}} \left( -2x-3y+4x+6y\right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{14}} \left( 2x+3y\right). \end{align}

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \require{cancel} \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S \\ &= \iint\limits_S \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{14}} \left( 2x+3y\right) \,\textrm{d}S \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{14}} \left( 2x+3y\right) \cdot ||\mathbf r_x \times \mathbf r_y|| \,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{14}} \left( 2x+3y\right) \cdot \sqrt{14}\,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \dfrac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{14}}} \left( 2x+3y\right) \cdot \cancel{\sqrt{14}}\,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D 2x+3y \,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \int_0^1 2x+3y \,\textrm{d}x\,\textrm d y \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \left[x^2+3xy\right]_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\textrm d y \\[5pt] &=\int_0^1 1+3y \,\textrm d y \\[5pt] &= \left[y+\dfrac32y^2\right]_0^1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac52 \\[5pt] \end{align*}

question.text:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \left\langle y,\: x,\: z \right\rangle$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=3x-y$ for $0\leq x\leq 1$ and $0\leq y\leq 2.$ Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ with respect to the downward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n.$

Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||\mathbf r_x \times \mathbf r_y|| = \sqrt{11}.$
question.explanation:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S. \]

Notice that our surface $z=3x-y$ can be written using the dot product as

\[ \langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\left\langle -3,\: 1, \: 1 \right\rangle}_{-\widetilde{\mathbf n}} = 0, \quad \textrm{or}\quad \langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\left\langle 3,\: -1, \: -1 \right\rangle}_{\widetilde{\mathbf n}} = 0. \]

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

\[ \widetilde{\mathbf n} = \left\langle 3,\: -1, \: -1 \right\rangle. \]

Normalizing this vector, we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf n &= \dfrac{\widetilde{\mathbf n}}{\Vert \widetilde{\mathbf n} \Vert} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{ \left\langle 3,\: -1, \: -1 \right\rangle}{\sqrt{3^2+(-1)^2+(-1)^2}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{11}}\langle 3,\: -1, \: -1 \rangle. \end{align*}

Using the fact that $z=3x-y$ on $S,$ we have

\begin{align} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} &= \left\langle y,\: x,\: z\right\rangle \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{11}}\langle 3,\: -1, \: -1 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{11}} \left\langle y,\: x,\: 3x-y \right\rangle \cdot \langle 3,\: -1, \: -1 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{11}} \left( 3y -x -(3x-y) \right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x). \end{align}

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S \\ &= \iint\limits_S \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x) \,\textrm{d}S \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x) \cdot ||\mathbf r_x \times \mathbf r_y|| \,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x)\cdot \sqrt{11}\,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \dfrac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{11}}}(4y-4x) \cdot \cancel{\sqrt{11}}\,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D (4y-4x)\,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^1 (4y-4x) \,\textrm d x \,\textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_0^2 \left[4xy - 2x^2\right]_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\textrm d y \\[5pt] &=\int_0^2 (4y-2)\,\textrm d y \\[5pt] & = \left[2y^2 - 2y\right]_{0}^2 \\[5pt] &= 4 \end{align*}

question.text:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \left\langle 3x,\: 2z,\: y-2 \right\rangle$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2x-y+1$ for $0\leq x\leq 4$ and $0\leq y\leq 1.$ Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ with respect to the downward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n.$

Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||\mathbf r_x \times \mathbf r_y|| =\sqrt{6}.$
question.explanation:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S. \]

Notice that our surface $z=2x-y+1$ can be written using the dot product as

\[ \langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\left\langle -2,\: 1, \: 1 \right\rangle}_{-\widetilde{\mathbf n}} = 1, \quad \textrm{or}\quad \langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\left\langle 2,\: -1, \: -1 \right\rangle}_{\widetilde{\mathbf n}} = -1. \]

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

\[ \widetilde{\mathbf n} = \left\langle 2,\: -1, \: -1 \right\rangle. \]

Normalizing this vector, we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf n &= \dfrac{\widetilde{\mathbf n}}{\Vert \widetilde{\mathbf n} \Vert} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{ \left\langle 2,\: -1, \: -1 \right\rangle}{\sqrt{2^2+(-1)^2+(-1)^2}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\langle 2,\: -1, \: -1 \rangle. \end{align*}

Using the fact that $z=2x -y +1$ on $S,$ we have

\begin{align} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} &= \left\langle 3x,\: 2z,\: y-2 \right\rangle \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\langle 2,\: -1, \: -1 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \left\langle 3x,\: 4x-2y+2,\: y-2 \right\rangle \cdot \langle 2,\: -1, \: -1 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \left( 6x -(4x -2y +2) - (y-2) \right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x +y). \end{align}

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S \\ &= \iint\limits_S \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x+y) \,\textrm{d}S \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x+y) \cdot ||\mathbf r_x \times \mathbf r_y|| \,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x+y)\cdot \sqrt{6}\,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \dfrac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{6}}}(2x+y) \cdot \cancel{\sqrt{6}}\,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D (2x+y)\,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^4 (2x+y) \,\textrm d x \,\textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \left[ x^2 + xy \right]_{x=0}^{x=4}\,\textrm d y \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 (4y+16)\,\textrm d y \\[5pt] & = \Big[2y^2 +16y\Big]_{0}^1 \\[5pt] &= 18 \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle y,\: z,\: 2x-y\rangle$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=3$ for $1\leq x\leq 2$ and $0\leq y\leq 1.$ Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ with respect to the downward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n.$
question.explanation:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S. \]

For the surface $z=3$ for $1\leq x\leq 2$ and $0\leq y\leq 1,$ the downward-pointing unit normal vector is

\[ \mathbf n = \langle 0,\, 0,\, -1\rangle. \]

Using the fact that $z=3$ on $S,$ we have

\begin{align} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} &= \left\langle y,\: z,\: 2x-y \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle 0,\:0,\: -1 \right\rangle\\[5pt] &= \left\langle y,\: 3,\: 2x-y \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle 0,\:0,\: -1 \right\rangle\\[5pt] &=-(2x-y). \end{align}

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S \\ &= \iint\limits_S (-(2x-y)) \,\textrm{d}S \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D (-(2x-y)) \,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \int_1^2 (-(2x-y)) \,\textrm{d}x\,\textrm d y \\[5pt] &= -\int_0^1 \left[\left(x^2-xy\right)\big|_{x=1}^{x=2}\,\right] \textrm d y \\[5pt] &= -\int_0^1 \left(3-y\right)\, \textrm d y \\[5pt] &=-\left[3y-\frac{y^2}{2}\right]_0^1 \\[5pt] &=-\frac52 \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle z,\: z,\: 4xy\rangle$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2$ for $0\leq x\leq 2$ and $0\leq y\leq 3.$ Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ with respect to the downward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n.$
question.explanation:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S. \]

For the surface $z=2$ for $0\leq x\leq 2$ and $0\leq y\leq 3,$ the downward-pointing unit normal vector is

\[ \mathbf n = \langle 0,\, 0,\, -1\rangle. \]

Using the fact that $z=2$ on $S,$ we have

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} &= \left\langle z,\: z,\: 4xy \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle 0,\:0,\: -1 \right\rangle\\[5pt] &=-4xy. \end{align*}

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S \\ &= \iint\limits_S (-4xy) \,\textrm{d}S \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D (-4xy) \,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \int_0^3 \int_0^2 (-4xy) \,\textrm{d}x\,\textrm d y \\[5pt] &= -\int_0^3 2y\, \textrm d y\int_0^2 2x \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=-\left[y^2\right]_0^3\cdot \left[ x^2\right]_0^2 \\[5pt] &=-36 \end{align*}
